cards.front: How is the vector $\vec{AB}$ expressed using the position vectors $\vec{OA}$ and $\vec{OB}$?

options.explanation: Subtracting the position vector of the starting point A from that of the endpoint B gives the displacement from A to B.
Reversing the subtraction gives the vector from B to A, which points in the opposite direction. The correct relationship is $\vec{AB} = \vec{OB} - \vec{OA}$.
Adding both position vectors does not represent the displacement between A and B. The starting position must be subtracted, giving $\vec{AB} = \vec{OB} - \vec{OA}$.
The sum of the two position vectors does not account for A being the starting point. Subtracting A’s position from B’s gives $\vec{AB} = \vec{OB} - \vec{OA}$.

cards.back: A vector that starts from the origin (point O).

options.text: A vector that starts from the origin (point O).
options.explanation: A position vector describes the location of a point relative to the origin, so its initial point is always the origin O.

options.text: A vector that ends at the origin (point O).
options.explanation: This reverses the defining direction of a position vector. A position vector starts at the origin O and ends at the point whose position it represents.

options.text: A vector that starts from any fixed point (point A).
options.explanation: Using any fixed starting point describes a general displacement vector, not necessarily a position vector. A position vector must start from the origin O.

options.text: A vector that joins any two points (points A and B).
options.explanation: A vector between arbitrary points represents displacement from one point to another. A position vector specifically begins at the origin O and locates another point.
